Q: Python treemap with first level as color and legend rather than labels A:

Thank you for your answer ! I'll try and clarify my question based on your examples.

My issue is that using the squarify package, the colors (what I call "first level") are not put into squares themselves, and it makes it difficult to order categories : in your example, I am unable to tell which of the orange and green category is bigger, which for me is the point of using a multi-level treemap.

I would like to make something similar to what you can get using R with the treemap package (see https://r-graph-gallery.com/235-treemap-with-subgroups.html), where the second level completely fills the first level (in plotly there is a first-level box that is bigger than the sum of second-level boxes)

Q: Compare Compiler Explorer and MSVC C++ version A:

You can look up version numbers here: Microsoft Visual C++ - Internal version numbering.

Compiler Explorer uses _MSC_VER separated by a dot, e.g. 1914 is 19.14 on Compiler Explorer.

Q: Enrichment analysis on Log2(tpm+1) RNA-seq A:

The industry standard for log2(tpm+1) data is still the limma package.

It was built for exactly this type of continuous normally distributed data.

It uses Empirical Bayes Trick to borrow information across all genes, which makes it's stats very robust, even if you only have a few samples (like 3 sick and 3 healthy patients).

Then use You can drop those results straight into fgsea (Fast Gene Set Enrichment Analysis).

But if you really want to Build a ML predictive model or a diagnostic tool that can look at a new patient's genes which will tell you, if they are sick or healthy, then Use WGCNA . Then feed those EigenGenes into a Penalized Regression Model like Elastic Net/Lasso Regression . Glymnet is the exact software package (originally in R, now available in Python too) that runs Lasso and Elastic Net regression.

Great to see you are involved in Medicine !!!

Q: Cannot filter by spatial extent a GTFS (gtfstools) A:

You need to order gtfs_list[["atm"]]$stop_times by trip_id & stop_sequence before running filter_by_spatial_extent(gtfs_list[["atm"]], stibm) on it. The fix is

gtfs_list <- lapply(gtfs_list, function(gtfs) {
  if (!is.null(gtfs$shapes) && nrow(gtfs$shapes) > 0) {
    shapes_dt <- as.data.table(gtfs$shapes)
    setorder(shapes_dt, shape_id, shape_pt_sequence)
    gtfs$shapes <- shapes_dt
    # Stop times need to be ordered by trip_id & stop_sequence!!
    stop_times_dt <- as.data.table(gtfs$stop_times)
    setorder(stop_times_dt, trip_id, stop_sequence)
    gtfs$stop_times <- stop_times_dt
  }
  
  return(gtfs)
})

Root cause

The error comes from this line in gtfstools::filter_by_spatial_extent()

trips_sf <- get_trip_geometry(gtfs_list[["atm"]], file = "stop_times")

which throws this error because of sort_sequence = FALSE

if unsorted runs into this issue (testthat of sfheaders:::rcpp_sf_linestring) or this related github issue:

Q: Python - XlsxWriter: Referring to columns by column name, not column letter (Hardcode vs. dynamic variable) A:

The best way to do this is to use the row/col notation form of data_validation() and use Pandas to get the index of the column and the dimensions of the dataframe. Something like this:

import pandas as pd


# Create a Pandas dataframe from some data.
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Data 1": [10, 20, 30, 20],
        "Data 2": [10, 20, 30, 20],
        "Block Status": ["unblocked", "blocked", "unblocked", "unblocked"],
        "Data 3": [10, 20, 30, 20],
        "Data 4": [10, 20, 30, 20],
    }
)

# Create a Pandas Excel writer using XlsxWriter as the engine.
writer = pd.ExcelWriter("pandas_example.xlsx", engine="xlsxwriter")

# Convert the dataframe to an XlsxWriter Excel object.
df.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Sheet1")

# Get the xlsxwriter workbook and worksheet objects.
workbook = writer.book
worksheet = writer.sheets["Sheet1"]

# Get the max row from the dimensions of the dataframe.
row_num = df.shape[0]

# Get the column index from the name. We add 1 to account for the index.
# If the index is turned off then this can be omitted.
col_num = 1 + df.columns.get_loc("Block Status")

# Add the data validation based on these dimensions.
worksheet.data_validation(
    1, col_num, row_num, col_num,
    {
        "validate": "list",
        "source": ["blocked", "unblocked"]
    },
)

# Close the Pandas Excel writer and output the Excel file.
writer.close()
